uses: Native Americans used purple coneflower for infections of the chest and throat, for toothache and for snakebite. In modern folk practice it is taken for a short time when a cold is starting. The fresh plant juice and root preparations are the traditional forms, and some salves made with it were dabbed on small cuts and grazes. Chewing the root gives a well-known tingling on the tongue.
taste: Faintly aromatic and sweetish, with a tingling feel in the mouth
caution_pregnancy: Some studies suggest use for up to 7 days in the first trimester may be safe, but ask a health care provider first. Little is known about use while breastfeeding. The EMA does not recommend it in pregnancy or nursing unless a doctor advises, and says echinacea skin products should not go on the breast while breastfeeding.
caution_medications: Evidence is mixed on whether echinacea affects drugs the liver breaks down. There are theoretical concerns about using it with immunosuppressants (drugs that damp down the immune system) and with caffeine. Talk with a health care provider before combining it with any medicine.
caution_conditions: Do not use it if you are allergic to daisy-family (Asteraceae) plants such as ragweed, sunflowers, daisies, chamomile or calendula. Allergic reactions can be severe, up to anaphylaxis, and people with allergic tendencies such as asthma, eczema or hay fever are at higher risk. The EMA advises against it with autoimmune disease, weakened or suppressed immunity, white blood cell disorders or progressive systemic illness. Not recommended for children under 12; some children in a trial developed rashes. Stomach pain and nausea are its most common side effects.
caution_duration: Short-term use only. The EMA limits use by mouth to 10 days and use on the skin to one week; see a doctor if symptoms worsen or a high fever appears.
caution_topical: Can cause rash, contact dermatitis, eczema and swelling of the lips. If a wound shows signs of infection, get medical advice.
garden_harvest_timing: Gather flowers and leaves while it blooms, roughly June to August. Leave some seed heads standing for the birds.
garden_water: Drought tolerant once established; likes well-drained loam
notes: A North American prairie native and a strong pollinator plant; goldfinches eat the seeds in winter, and native bees nest in the hollow dead stems, so cut stems back to a foot or two and leave them standing. Wild coneflowers have declined from illegal root-digging for the herb trade, so grow your own or buy cultivated root. Culpeper never knew this plant and gives it no planet.
